notes:
I've written up notes on Revelation 2 from the sources I could reach. Some limits first. I didn't get to read netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org or any Lutheran site. Only part of three key pages came through: Enduring Word stops after v. 7, Constable stops at v. 10, and the Cambridge commentary stops partway through v. 20. So vv. 21–28 rest on short search previews. I found nothing on v. 28 (the morning star) or on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings, so those are left out.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Who is the "angel"? Guzik says it may be the pastor or an angel watching over the church. Either way it stands for the church, and the letter is meant for everyone in it. The images show that Jesus has authority over the church (he holds the stars) and is present in it (he walks among the lampstands). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-2/
- Constable thinks the angel was most likely a human messenger who carried the letter and read it to the church. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-2.html
- Clarke takes the angel as the messenger, the pastor, sent by Christ and his apostles to teach and edify that Church. https://studylight.org/commentaries/acc/revelation-2.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says "The angel" seems to be the spirit of the Church personified as its responsible guardian. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/revelation-2.html

**vv. 2–3:** Jesus knows the church's real condition. They worked hard and kept going (the Greek word means "steadfast endurance"). They took Paul's warning about "wolves" in Acts 20 seriously. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-2/
- Constable thinks the false apostles were travelling teachers claiming apostolic rank. He also notes that the early church fathers recognised no apostles beyond the New Testament ones. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-2.html

**v. 4:** Guzik stresses that they *left* their first love; they didn't just *lose* it. Leaving is deliberate. Probably both love for God and love for each other are meant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-2/
- Constable thinks love for Christ is in view, though many commentators (e.g., Stott) read it as love for one another. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-2.html
- The Cambridge commentary suggests married love may be the picture (compare Jeremiah 2:2). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/revelation-2.html

**v. 5:** There are three steps: remember, repent, and do the first works. Losing the lampstand would mean the group might carry on as an organisation but no longer be a true church. Ignatius later praised the Ephesian church, which suggests it listened. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-2/
- Cambridge comments that Jesus doesn't say "love again," because love isn't directly under our control. He says "do the first works," because that is. Cambridge doubts that the later Turkish destruction of Ephesus was the fulfilment of this warning. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/revelation-2.html

**v. 6:** Most writers follow Irenaeus: the Nicolaitans lived lives of unrestrained indulgence. Benson repeats the tradition that they began with Nicolas, one of the seven deacons mentioned Acts 6:5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/2-6.htm
- Constable quotes Tenney: their teaching was an exaggeration of the doctrine of Christian liberty which attempted an ethical compromise with heathenism. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-2.html
- Guzik's point: the God of love hates sin and wants his people to hate it too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-2/

**v. 7:** The tree of life in God's paradise recalls Genesis 2–3 and points ahead to Revelation 22. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-2.html
- Cambridge notes that the call to "hear" covers the whole letter, not just the closing promise. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/revelation-2.html

**v. 8:** Constable explains that "Smyrna" is linked to myrrh, a spice used in burials. The city itself had been destroyed and rebuilt, so Christ as the one who "died and returned to life" fitted these readers well. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-2.html

**v. 9:** Constable thinks persecution was cutting off the Christians' income. He has no rebuke for this church. He also records the tradition that Jews helped at Polycarp's martyrdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-2.html
- Cambridge reads "slander" as rough lies about the believers. It says the opponents were real Jews by birth whom Christ calls unworthy of the name. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/revelation-2.html

**v. 10:** Readings of "ten days" vary:
- a short time;
- ten persecutions under Roman emperors;
- an undefined period of trial.

Constable lists these, and also explains that Roman prisons were used to force compliance, not as a punishment in themselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-2.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says "be faithful" literally means become thou faithful; show thyself to be such. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/revelation-2.html
- Cambridge takes the crown of life to be eternal life pictured as a royal crown. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/revelation-2.html

**v. 11:** Cambridge only points ahead to the "second death" in Revelation 20:6 and 20:14. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/revelation-2.html

**vv. 12–13:** Christ mentions the sword because he threatens to use it in v. 16. For "Satan's throne," suggestions include the worship of Asclepius (the serpent god) and the great altar of Zeus. Cambridge prefers to read it as Pergamum being a centre of persecution. It also says almost nothing reliable is known about Antipas beyond this verse. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/revelation-2.html
- Clarke mentions a later story that Antipas was put to death by being enclosed in a burning brazen bull. https://studylight.org/commentaries/acc/revelation-2.html
- A Precept Austin source calls him the first Christian put to death by the Roman state. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-2-commentary

**vv. 14–15:** Commentators disagree on whether the Balaam group and the Nicolaitans were one group or two.
- Cambridge says one group: Balaam taught it long ago, and the Nicolaitans teach the same now. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/revelation-2.html
- Ellicott sees Balaam's story as an illustration of the Nicolaitan temptation, with Both temptations lead in the same Antinomian direction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/2-15.htm
- Another commentator on the same page thinks in Revelation 2:14, the Balaamites are evidently distinguished from the Nicolaitans. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/2-6.htm

**v. 16:** The whole church must repent because it tolerated what Ephesus refused to tolerate. Note that the threat is "against them," not against the whole church. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/revelation-2.html

**v. 17:**
- Cambridge sees the hidden manna as the pot of manna kept in the Ark, and as God's bread in place of meals at idols' tables. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/revelation-2.html
- Barnes: almost no two expositors agree on the white stone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/2-17.htm
- Suggested meanings of the white stone include a vote for acquittal, an admission token (*tessera*), the high priest's gems, and a victor's award. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/2-17.html
- Gill reads it as justification and adoption, gifts of free grace, and not owing to the works and merit of men. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/2-17.html

**vv. 18–19:** "Son of God" anticipates the authority from the Father promised in v. 27. The blazing eyes search hearts (v. 23). Unlike Ephesus, this church's later works are greater than its first. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/revelation-2.html

**v. 20:** Some manuscripts read "thy wife Jezebel." Cambridge treats that as possible but difficult. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/revelation-2.html
- Barclay's comment as quoted on StudyLight: Jezebel was clearly a member of the church, working from inside. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/2-20.html
- Desiring God sums up the problem as worldliness — compromise with the world. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/poisonous-tolerance
- The Geneva notes say Often in the scripture, by fornication they mean idolatry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/2-20.htm

**v. 21:** Guzik draws out both God's mercy in giving her time and his judgment when that time is refused. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-2/

**v. 23:** The Pulpit Commentary says "minds and hearts" together mean something like "the devices and desires of our own hearts." Here the Lord turns from the angel to individuals in the church. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/revelation-2.html

**v. 24:** Who calls them "the deep things of Satan"? The Pulpit Commentary weighs whether it was the faithful mocking the teaching or the false teachers themselves, and finds the first option rather tame in meaning. https://biblehub.com/revelation/2-24.htm
- Barclay says some heretics taught it was a duty to experience every kind of sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/2-20.html
- Guzik suggests the reasoning may have been that you must learn Satan's depths in order to defeat him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-2/

**v. 27:** In a Pulpit Commentary homily, Christ the Shepherd feeds and leads his own and breaks the opposers' power. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/revelation-2.html

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

The pages below didn't usually name the writers' denominations, so these are grouped by issue, not by church.

- **Who the "overcomer" is (vv. 7, 11, 17, 26):** Constable lists many (Chafer, Ryrie, Walvoord, Stott, Ladd, Beale) who say it means every true Christian. Others (Barnhouse, Hodges, Dillow and more) say it means only faithful Christians. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-2.html
- **Do the seven churches stand for seven ages of church history?**
  - Constable thinks the order of the letters has proved prophetic, though the text doesn't say so, and links Ephesus with the apostolic age. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-2.html
  - MacArthur says chapters 2–3 describe the present age, the church age. https://www.gty.org/sermons/81-160/the-lords-indictment-of-unfaithful-churches
  - Precept Austin rejects the church-ages view; it notes proponents can't agree on which periods are meant or their dates. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-topics-seven_churches
  - Sam Storms describes the view; he quotes Tenney's criticism that historicist readings largely ignore the church outside Europe. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/an-introduction-to-the-book-of-revelation---part-ii
  - Ligonier: Few interpreters of Revelation are historicists today. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/john-and-the-seven-churches
  - Gill reads v. 17 partly through this lens, with references to the dark times of Popery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/2-17.htm
- **Pastor or bishop (v. 1)?** Doddridge, quoted in Benson, says each church had one presiding pastor, but this can by no means be proved to mean a diocesan bishop. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/2-1.htm
- **Nicolaitans as a "ruling the people" party (v. 6):** Newell reads the name as a laity-bossing clerisy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wnc/revelation-2.html Chuck Smith applies it to the "shepherding" movement within the Pentecostal churches. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/2-6.html
- **Who is to blame in Thyatira (v. 20):** Precept Austin quotes Adrian Rogers, who places the blame mainly on the pastor, because he allowed that woman Jezebel to teach. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-2-commentary

## 3. Other views

- **Catholic, on the "angel" (v. 1):** Catholic.com argues the angels are best read as bishops, because they are being praised or rebuked for the state of each of their churches. It uses this as evidence for single bishops leading early churches. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/blog/when-bishops-are-literal-angels
- Haydock names Timothy as the angel of Ephesus. He adds that the rebukes are aimed at members of the church, not at Timothy personally. For Smyrna he names St. Polycarp, or some bishop there before him. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/revelation-2.html
- Against Polycarp being the angel of Smyrna: Ellicott thinks it would require his time as bishop to have lasted about 60 years, which seems unlikely. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/2-8.htm
- **Catholic, on church ages:** Jimmy Akin argues the seven-ages idea isn't in the text, and that its dates keep shifting so the teacher always lives in the final age. https://www.catholic.com/audio/tjap/jesus-graded-7-churches-heres-the-report-card
- **Catholic, on v. 17:** Haydock reads the hidden manna as the joy of heaven, and the white stone and new name as a mark of the happiness promised to those who overcome. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/2-17.html
